title: Why is Chinese art being stolen?
summary: Hosts examine the string of thefts and heists of Chinese antiquities from Western and other foreign museums since 2010, asking whether the Chinese government is behind them. They trace background: the Century of Humiliation, the 1860 looting and burning of the Old Summer Palace (Yuanmingyuan), and the Chinese zodiac water-clock fountain heads. They cover China's repatriation push, billionaire collectors, the booming Chinese art market, and the Stockholm (Drottningholm), Oslo-area (Museum of Far Eastern Antiquities, Norway), Fitzwilliam/Durham (England), Fontainebleau (France, 2015), and Geneva (2019) heists, plus the debate over museum repatriation of looted art. The episode closes with listener mail about swamp coolers and a brief mention of upcoming films.

segments.title: Opening and framing the Chinese art heists
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the topic of Chinese art heists from world-class museums and the GQ article by Alex Palmer, asking whether the Chinese government is behind them or whether the booming market drives the thefts.

segments.title: Century of Humiliation and Mao's Four Olds
segments.summary: Background on the Century of Humiliation, Opium Wars and foreign powers' treaties, Mao's 1949 framing of the period, and the Cultural Revolution's destruction of relics known as the Four Olds.

segments.title: The Old Summer Palace looting and burning
segments.summary: The Yuanmingyuan (Old Summer Palace), built in 1709, was looted and burned by British and French forces in 1860 after the torture deaths of a negotiating delegation; the ruins were preserved as a reminder.

segments.title: Looted treasures in Europe and the zodiac fountain heads
segments.summary: Looted items ended up with European royals, including Queen Victoria's Pekinese dog Lootie. The zodiac water-clock fountain heads from the Summer Palace became a major symbol of the looting.

segments.title: China's repatriation drive and billionaire collectors
segments.summary: As China grew economically, it began seeking to recover antiquities as heritage. Chinese billionaires bought collections and opened private museums, and the Chinese art market grew to around a billion dollars a year by 2018. UNESCO figures on objects held abroad are cited.

segments.title: Zodiac head auctions and the Poly Group
segments.summary: The China Poly Group's culture wing Poly Culture pursued artifacts. Sotheby's and Christie's auctioned zodiac heads in 2000, and China's pressure in 2009 led Christie's to hand over two heads from the Saint Laurent estate. A 2010 vase sold for nearly 70 million dollars after an 800,000 dollar presale estimate.

segments.title: Lu Yang's search and museums quietly removing listings
segments.summary: Chinese treasure hunter Lu Yang traveled to museums abroad identifying Summer Palace objects; some museums quietly removed web mentions, while the Fontainebleau held firm. The heists began in 2010.

segments.title: Stockholm and Norway museum heists
segments.summary: In August 2010 thieves smashed cases at Drottningholm Palace's Chinese pavilion in Stockholm in six minutes and escaped by moped and boat. Later, the Museum of Far Eastern Antiquities in Oslo (Norway) was robbed through a glass ceiling, with 56 objects taken, many from a Norwegian officer's collection; the China collection was later closed for renovation. A tip suggested an object was in a Shanghai airport, but Norway did not pursue it.

segments.title: Cambridge and Durham heists and hired thieves
segments.summary: In April 2012 the Fitzwilliam Museum in Cambridge lost 18 items and the Durham University Oriental Museum lost two items worth about three million dollars. Durham thieves were caught after a witness and a cell phone helped police, and the gang was linked to the Rathkeel Rovers, Irish travelers. Hosts note the thieves seemed to be hired criminals, with a Chinese connection in Donald Wong.

segments.title: Fontainebleau 2015 and Geneva 2019 heists
segments.summary: Thieves broke into the Fontainebleau outside Paris in March 2015, taking about fifteen objects including a replica of the King of Siam's crown; some were arrested. In June 2019 a museum in Geneva lost Ming dynasty items in under a minute, and British suspects were caught. Operation Bamboo foiled a planned robbery and suspects said they were hired by the Chinese mafia.

segments.title: Chinese government stance and heist motives
segments.summary: Hosts discuss that the investigations never reached the top figures, that the Chinese government has denied involvement, and that Poly Culture's manager called the GQ story nonsense. China reportedly treats all such objects as illegitimate and discourages theft mainly because items may be damaged.

segments.title: Museum repatriation debate
segments.summary: Hosts discuss repatriation claims from China, Greece and Nigeria, museums arguing they can care better for objects, a British Museum curator's theft of thousands of pieces sold on eBay, UK law limiting repatriation, and exceptions for divided or unstable cultural heritage.

segments.title: Upcoming films on art theft
segments.summary: Hosts mention an upcoming Netflix adaptation of Grace D. Lee's novel Portrait of a Thief and a 2012 Jackie Chan film about art theft.

segments.title: Listener mail on swamp coolers
segments.summary: A listener from Santa Fe describes using a portable swamp cooler at high elevation and praises whole-house swamp coolers as more energy efficient than AC.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listener emails and sign off.
